question:
Patient note:
A 71-year-old man is evaluated early this morning on the surgical ward in anticipation of a laparoscopic sigmoid resection scheduled for later today to address a high-grade stricture discovered during colonoscopy two months ago; the colorectal team estimates three ports, two hours of operative time under general anesthesia, and an anticipated overnight stay in the step-down unit. He was transferred from the medical service after a complicated admission that began twenty-one days ago when he arrived through the emergency department febrile to 39.2 °C with shaking chills, diffuse abdominal discomfort, and systolic blood pressures in the low 90s. Blood cultures from that encounter grew Escherichia coli in both aerobic bottles, and cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a contained sigmoid diverticular perforation with surrounding phlegmon. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, resuscitation with balanced crystalloids, and CT-guided percutaneous drainage of a 5-cm pelvic abscess led to gradual defervescence, but he remained hemodynamically labile for the first 48 hours and required a right internal jugular triple-lumen catheter placed by the critical care team for vasopressor support and high-volume fluid administration; that line remains in situ today, covered by an intact transparent dressing with no erythema, tenderness, or discharge at the entry site, and all maintenance infusions continue to run through it. Since transfer out of the intensive care unit twelve days ago his clinical status has stabilized, yet his activity level has been markedly curtailed: nursing flow sheets document that he spends nearly the entire day recumbent, rising only with assistance to a bedside commode, and he has not walked the corridor because doing so precipitates light-headedness and concern for dislodging the pelvic drain that was removed only yesterday. He has required no splints, casts, or traction devices, has had no recent fractures or orthopedic injuries, and denies any vehicular collisions, falls, or multi-system trauma. Past medical history includes well-controlled hypertension on amlodipine, stage 3 chronic kidney disease with a baseline creatinine between 1.4 and 1.6 mg/dL, and benign prostatic hyperplasia treated with tamsulosin. He has never been diagnosed with heart failure, chronic lung disease, systemic inflammatory bowel disorders, or any form of cancer, and a transthoracic echocardiogram obtained last year for palpitations showed normal ventricular size and function with an ejection fraction of 60 %. He recalls no prior episodes of clot in the legs or lungs, has never required lifelong anticoagulation, and duplex sonography has not been performed during this admission because his calves remain symmetric, warm, and nontender without dilated superficial veins or pitting edema. He does, however, volunteer that two siblings developed venous thromboses in middle age—one brother experienced a lower-limb clot after knee replacement and the other suffered a pulmonary embolus while recuperating from pneumonia—which has made him “nervous about clots,” although he has not pursued formal genetic testing. He has never been told that he carries antiphospholipid antibodies, factor II mutation, or other inherited thrombophilias, and previous routine laboratories have shown normal platelet counts without episodes suggestive of heparin-related immune thrombocytopenia. He completed a 14-day course of intravenous piperacillin–tazobactam for the diverticular infection, after which antimicrobial therapy was transitioned to oral levofloxacin and metronidazole two days ago; he remains afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Review of systems is otherwise negative for cough, sputum production, exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, vision change, headache, bowel habit alteration beyond known constipation, or urinary urgency. He quit a 20-pack-year cigarette history two decades ago and drinks a glass of red wine with dinner but denies recreational drug use. On examination he lies supine in bed appearing comfortable and oriented. Vital signs: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, pulse 84 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air. Body mass index is 26 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsations are 3 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, and S1/S2 are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Lungs are clear to auscultation with good air entry bilaterally. The abdomen shows a well-healed 1-cm scar at the prior drain site in the left lower quadrant with no surrounding induration; there is mild tenderness over the sigmoid colon but no rebound or guarding, and bowel sounds are normoactive. Lower extremities are of equal circumference, free of cords or varicosities, and painless on dorsiflexion. Neurologic examination reveals full strength and intact sensation in all extremities. Skin is warm, dry, and without petechiae or ecchymoses. Laboratory data drawn this morning via the central line show hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL, hematocrit 39 %, leukocytes 7.8 × 10⁹/L, platelets 232 × 10⁹/L, sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, AST 28 U/L, ALT 26 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 96 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an INR of 1.1, and activated partial thromboplastin time 31 s. A twelve-lead electrocardiogram displays normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats/min without ST-T abnormalities, and a portable chest radiograph taken yesterday shows clear lung fields with the catheter tip projecting at the lower superior vena cava. Sequential compression sleeves are at the bedside but have not been applied because the patient complains they feel tight; no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has yet been initiated pending final operative timing. He has been kept nil per os since midnight, renal-adjusted preoperative antibiotics are planned for induction, and anesthesia anticipates straightforward airway management with a Mallampati class II view and full neck extension.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
Apply the Caprini surgical VTE risk assessment at the preoperative evaluation:
- Age 61–74 years: age 71 = 2.
- Laparoscopic surgery >45 minutes: planned 2-hour sigmoid resection = 2.
- Bed confinement >72 hours: nearly continuously recumbent for at least 12 days, apart from assisted commode use = 2.
- Central venous access: right internal jugular catheter still in place = 2.
- Sepsis within 1 month: bacteremic diverticular perforation with hypotension 21 days ago = 1.
- Family history of VTE: two affected siblings = 3, counted once. No personal VTE or known thrombophilia = 0 additional points.
The BMI threshold matters: the 2005 Caprini model adds 1 for BMI >25, giving 13 at BMI 26. With an obesity cutoff of BMI ≥30, BMI contributes 0, and the sum is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 + 0 = 12.
Final answer: 12
